strengths: Clear and significant problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing open-world 3D part segmentation methods inherit 2D SAM supervision, limiting them to surface-only understanding and uncontrollable clustering—and proposes the first feed-forward, promptable part segmentation model trained natively on 3D supervision.

Well-motivated architecture: the dual-branch triplane encoder (frozen PartField branch preserving SAM-derived 2D priors + learnable branch for native 3D adaptation, with zero-conv injection of normals/RGB) is a sensible and effective design for scaling, and the SAM-style prompt-guided decoder with multiple output tokens and IoU head is well adapted to 3D ambiguity.

Scalable data engine: the two-stage curation pipeline (scene-graph/connectivity-based labels on Objaverse plus a model-in-the-loop annotation scheme that filters PartField pseudo-labels via interactive IoU@1/IoU@10 criteria) is a thoughtful contribution that scales supervision to ~500k shapes and 5M+ parts; the filtering rationale is intuitive and visualized.

Strong empirical results: large improvements over strong baselines (91% relative IoU@1 gain over Point-SAM; >20% IoU gain over the second-best method for automatic segmentation on PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE), backed by convincing qualitative comparisons including AI-generated meshes and interior/occluded structures that 2D-lifted methods fundamentally cannot capture.

Reasonably thorough appendix: ablations over encoder variants (Point-SAM encoder, frozen/learnable PartField) and training data variants support the two central design claims; the connectivity-leakage analysis (Table 4) is a commendably careful evaluation decision; complexity analysis and applications (interior editing, amodal segmentation with HoloPart) add value; limitations are honestly discussed (no semantic labels).
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination is not explicitly addressed: training data is curated from Objaverse, and PartObjaverse-Tiny is also drawn from Objaverse. The paper discusses leakage via mesh connectivity but does not state whether any training shapes overlap the evaluation sets (or report results on a filtered/disjoint split). This is an important omission for a foundation-model claim.

The 'Segment Every Part' mode depends on a hand-tuned NMS threshold T as a granularity hyperparameter; sensitivity to T and comparison under matched granularity settings across methods are not analyzed, making the automatic-segmentation comparison somewhat protocol-dependent.

Baselines are evaluated under modified settings (e.g., PartField with K-Means instead of its connectivity-based clustering) which the authors justify, but this weakens direct comparability with previously reported numbers; a table in the original protocol would strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility is limited: code/model 'will be released soon' rather than available, and the 5M-pair dataset pipeline involves multiple heuristic thresholds (IoU@1>60 / IoU@10>90, shape validity of >5 valid masks, component size filters) whose sensitivity is not ablated.

Several claims are qualitative only (e.g., superiority on hierarchical segmentation in Fig. 8, robustness on AI-generated meshes) without quantitative metrics such as boundary precision or human study; the interactive evaluation protocol also follows an idealized oracle prompt selection rather than real user behavior.

The model inherits limitations from its frozen PartField branch and point-click-only prompts; text/box prompting and semantic labeling are absent, which limits practical utility relative to the 'foundation model' framing, though this is acknowledged.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: promptable, open-world 3D part segmentation trained natively in 3D, rather than lifting 2D SAM masks.
The scale of the data effort is appreciable: a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline that expands supervision to ~500k shapes and 5M+ shape-part pairs is a substantial engineering contribution.

Quantitative results show large margins over existing baselines (e.g., ~91% relative IoU@1 improvement over Point-SAM, >20% IoU gain in automatic segmentation), supported by qualitative comparisons on both curated benchmarks and AI-generated meshes.

Appendix includes ablations over encoder variants and training data, a complexity analysis, applications (interior part editing, amodal segmentation with HoloPart), and a discussion of the mesh-connectivity label leakage issue in PartObjaverse-Tiny.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially the SAM recipe (promptable encoder-decoder, parallel decoding, IoU head, interactive prompt simulation) transplanted to 3D, with a triplane representation borrowed from Chan et al. and a frozen PartField encoder reused almost verbatim. The core architectural contribution is a combination of well-known components, and the 'emergent open-world capability' framing overstates what is a straightforward consequence of scale.

Potential train/test contamination is not adequately addressed. The training corpus is built from Objaverse, and the primary quantitative benchmark (PartObjaverse-Tiny) is also derived from Objaverse. The paper discusses label leakage via mesh connectivity but never reports de-duplication or overlap statistics between the 500k training shapes and the benchmark. Given the magnitude of the reported gains, this is a serious validity concern.

Circularity in the data pipeline: the model is trained with a frozen PartField encoder while simultaneously using PartField outputs as pseudo-labels filtered by the model's own interactive IoU criterion. This self-referential annotation loop risks reinforcing PartField's biases and inflating consistency with the evaluation protocol, and no independent human verification of annotation quality is provided.

Evaluation scope is narrow: quantitative results are confined to PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, both of which are artist meshes with relatively clean connectivity. There is no quantitative evaluation on scanned or real-world data, and no text-prompted or hierarchical segmentation metrics despite claims of broad applicability.

Key supporting material (ablations, complexity analysis, limitations) is relegated to the appendix, leaving the main paper short on critical analysis. The 'Discussions' section in the main text merely points to the appendix.

Reproducibility is weak: code and model are only promised ('will be released soon'), the 5M-pair dataset curation pipeline depends on PartField checkpoints and several heuristic thresholds (IoU@1 > 60, IoU@10 > 90, component size filtering, NMS threshold T) whose sensitivity is not analyzed.

The comparison against PartField disables its mesh connectivity in the main table, which disadvantages it; while the appendix justifies this and includes a connectivity-enabled comparison, the headline claims are built on the modified protocol and the baseline tuning is not fully transparent.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the first promptable, feed-forward 3D part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data, addressing real limitations of 2D-lifting approaches (surface-only understanding, no interior structure, uncontrollable clustering-based decomposition).

Strong empirical results with large margins: +91% relative IoU@1 improvement over Point-SAM on interactive segmentation and >20% IoU improvement over the second-best method (PartField*) on automatic segmentation across two benchmarks, supported by convincing qualitative comparisons on both artist meshes and AI-generated shapes.

A valuable and reusable data contribution: a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline that scales supervision from ~180k shapes/2M parts to 500k shapes/5M+ parts using PartField candidates filtered by an interactive IoU-based validity criterion, which could benefit future 3D part-understanding research.

Solid ablation studies in the appendix that cleanly separate the contribution of the dual-branch (frozen PartField + learnable) triplane encoder from the contribution of training data scale/diversity, plus the interesting finding about mesh-connectivity label leakage in PartObjaverse-Tiny (Table 4).

Good breadth of analysis: complexity comparison, downstream applications (interior part editing, amodal segmentation with HoloPart), additional visualizations, and an honest discussion of limitations (no semantic labels).

The design is sensible and well-engineered: SAM-style promptable decoder with ambiguity handling (multiple masks + IoU head), triplane representation for scalability, and preservation of 2D priors via a frozen branch.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination is not clearly addressed: the training corpus is curated from Objaverse, and PartObjaverse-Tiny is itself built from Objaverse assets. The paper discusses leakage through mesh connectivity but does not report whether test shapes (or near-duplicates) appear in the 500k-shape training set. This materially affects the interpretation of the headline numbers and should be explicitly quantified (e.g., deduplication statistics).

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two benchmarks (PartObjaverse-Tiny, ~200 shapes, and PartNetE) are used for quantitative evaluation, and both are relatively small. No quantitative results on held-out AI-generated shapes, no cross-dataset generalization experiment, and no evaluation of prompt robustness (e.g., prompts near boundaries, extreme part granularity).

Circularity concerns in the data pipeline: the frozen encoder branch is initialized from PartField, and PartField is also used to generate the pseudo-labels that supervise the learnable branch at scale. The paper does not analyze whether this biases the model toward PartField-style decomposition or measure the quality of the model-in-the-loop labels beyond IoU-based filtering heuristics.

Component-level novelty is limited: the triplane encoder, frozen-vs-learnable dual-branch design, decoder, losses, and interactive training simulation are each adapted from existing work (PartField, SAM, Point-SAM). The primary novelty is the combination and the data engine, which is legitimate but should be stated more precisely rather than framed as architectural innovation.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: code and model are only promised ('will be released soon'), and the curated dataset release is not committed. Given that the data pipeline is a central contribution, the paper's significance is conditional on this release. Key details (e.g., exact filtering thresholds, IoU computation for pseudo-labels, FPS/N_c ablation) are underspecified.

Interactive-segmentation comparison to Point-SAM may be somewhat favorable by construction: Point-SAM was trained on rendered ShapeNet data, whereas PartSAM's training distribution (Objaverse assets, possibly overlapping the test set) is much closer to the evaluation data. A fairer comparison would include a training-data-matched control.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'emergent open-world capabilities' and 'decisive step toward foundation models' rest on evaluations against methods with weaker training data, and no scaling-law-style analysis (e.g., performance vs. training corpus size) is provided to support the scalability narrative.

The 'Segment Every Part' mode introduces several heuristics (NMS threshold T, mask count settings, candidate filtering) whose sensitivity is only partially explored; no comparison of automatic pipelines with matched compute/budget is given.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated positioning: the paper identifies concrete limitations of 2D-lifting approaches (surface-only supervision, no interior structure, per-shape optimization cost) and proposes a native-3D, SAM-like promptable alternative, which is a meaningful step toward a 3D part segmentation foundation model.

Strong empirical results with large margins: +91% relative IoU over Point-SAM with a single prompt (Table 1) and >20% IoU improvement over the second-best method in automatic segmentation (Table 2), evaluated on standard benchmarks (PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNetE) plus additional 3DCoMPaT++ evaluation.

Scalable model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline producing ~5M shape-part pairs is a substantial engineering contribution, and the scaling curve (Figure 11) provides evidence that performance continues to improve with data size.

Thoughtful evaluation hygiene: the authors identify and correct a potential label-leakage issue in PartField's use of mesh connectivity on PartObjaverse-Tiny (Table 4, A.2.5), and justify their modified protocol with quantitative evidence.

Comprehensive appendix: architecture and data ablations (Table 3), complexity/runtime analysis (Table 5), cross-shape consistency, applications (interior editing, amodal segmentation with HoloPart), and honest failure-case analysis (Figure 14, A.2.8).
Good reproducibility signals: detailed hyperparameters, training setup, and decoding details in the appendix; project page promised for released resources.
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination is not addressed: the training corpus is curated from Objaverse(-XL), while the primary benchmark PartObjaverse-Tiny is also drawn from Objaverse. The paper never reports whether test shapes overlap training shapes, which directly undermines the headline 'open-world generalization' claims; a de-duplicated or unseen-source evaluation is needed.

Substantial dependence on prior work reduces perceived novelty: the encoder architecture is built directly on PartField's triplane/PVCNN design with pretrained initialization, and the data pipeline uses PartField outputs as pseudo-labels. The core novel element is largely the SAM-style decoder plus the annotation pipeline, making the contribution more incremental than 'first foundation model' framing suggests.

Circularity concerns in the data pipeline: pseudo-labels generated by PartField (with artist connectivity cues) are filtered by PartSAM's own predictions, then PartSAM trained on these labels is compared against PartField; the bias this introduces is analyzed only qualitatively.

Evaluation of automatic segmentation modifies baseline protocols (K-Means clustering without connectivity for PartField, best-of-multiple-masks for multi-scale baselines), which, while justified, makes headline numbers not directly comparable to previously reported results.
The model produces class-agnostic masks only; no semantic labeling capability, limiting applicability compared to text-driven open-vocabulary methods, and this limitation is deferred to future work.
Missing quantitative comparison on AI-generated meshes (Hunyuan3D) — this setting is only qualitative (Figures 7-9), despite being a key claimed advantage (robustness to broken connectivity).

Some missing details for full reproducibility: hyperparameters for automatic segmentation (NMS threshold choices, Nf), the effect of the three output tokens, and dataset release/ licensing status are not fully specified in the main text.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: promptable, open-world 3D part segmentation trained on native 3D supervision rather than lifted 2D masks, addressing real limitations of clustering-based and lifting-based methods (e.g., inability to capture interior/occluded structures).

Impressive scale of the data contribution: a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline yielding ~500k shapes / 5M+ native 3D shape–part pairs, with a described two-stage curation process and filtering criteria.

Strong empirical results: large gains over Point-SAM on interactive segmentation (e.g., 56.1 vs 29.4 IoU@1 on PartObjaverse-Tiny) and over multiple SOTA baselines on automatic segmentation, plus scaling-curve evidence and ablations of encoder variants and training data.

Good evaluation hygiene in places: the authors identify and correct a label-leakage issue with mesh connectivity in PartObjaverse-Tiny, provide complexity/runtime analysis, qualitative comparisons on AI-generated meshes, failure cases, and a 3DCoMPaT++ evaluation.
Reasonably complete technical description in the appendix (architecture details, hyperparameters, training procedure), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential train–test contamination is not convincingly addressed: the training corpus is drawn from Objaverse, and the primary benchmark PartObjaverse-Tiny is itself a subset of Objaverse. The paper never explicitly states that evaluation shapes were excluded from the 500k training shapes, and given the model-in-the-loop pipeline iterates over 'over-fragmented' Objaverse assets, leakage risk is substantial. This undermines the headline claims.

Partial circularity in supervision and representation: the encoder is initialized from and partially frozen at PartField (which itself distills SAM via 2D lifting), and the second-stage 'native 3D' labels are generated by PartField clustering filtered by PartSAM's own predictions. Claims of being 'trained natively on 3D data beyond 2D supervision' are therefore stronger than the evidence; a large fraction of the effective supervision still traces back to 2D SAM.

Limited architectural novelty: the design is essentially SAM's promptable decoder transplanted onto PartField's triplane encoder, with known components (PVCNN, two-way transformer, parallel output tokens, IoU head, zero conv). The main contribution is the data engine rather than methodological innovation.

Discrepancies and incomplete reporting: ablation Table 3 numbers (e.g., Ours IoU@3=79.0, IoU@5=84.7) do not match Table 1 (78.3, 84.1) without explanation; ablation comparisons to Point-SAM are retrained by the authors under unspecified conditions, making the 'architecture scales better' claim hard to verify.
The 'first promptable 3D part segmentation model' claim is overstated given Point-SAM (ICLR 2025) and iSeg; positioning should be more careful.

The PartField* baseline in Table 2 is evaluated in a deliberately weakened setting (K-Means without connectivity), and while the authors justify this, the comparison protocol differs across baselines (SAMesh with connectivity, PartField without), complicating interpretation of the reported margins.

Scalability claims rest on a 40k→500k scaling curve with 8×H20 GPU training; compute cost, dataset release plans, and licensing of Objaverse-derived annotations are not discussed, limiting reproducibility and impact assessment.

strengths: Clear and significant contribution: the first promptable part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data, moving beyond the dominant paradigm of lifting 2D SAM masks to 3D. This addresses a genuine limitation of prior work (surface-only understanding, inability to capture interior/occluded structures), and the results support the claim convincingly.

Strong quantitative results with large margins: +26.7 IoU@1 over Point-SAM on PartObjaverse-Tiny interactive segmentation, and >12 points over the second-best method in automatic segmentation on both benchmarks, plus additional evaluation on 3DCoMPaT++.

Well-designed dual-branch encoder (frozen SAM-prior branch + learnable native-3D branch) is well-motivated and validated by ablations: the paper carefully disentangles the contributions of pretrained priors (w/o pretrain, frozen vs. learnable PartField, catastrophic forgetting analysis) and training data (PartNet-only, Stage-1 curated, full model-in-the-loop).

The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is a valuable contribution in itself, producing 5M shape-part pairs with an automated quality filter (IoU@1>60 or IoU@10>90), and the scaling curve (40k-500k shapes) provides evidence that the approach genuinely benefits from data scale rather than saturating.

Thoughtful and honest evaluation practice: the paper identifies and corrects a label-leakage issue in evaluating PartField on PartObjaverse-Tiny (mesh connectivity correlates with ground-truth labels; Table 4 shows a random feature model with connectivity achieves 65.6), justifying the modified protocol with quantitative evidence. Failure cases, limitations (long-tail part distribution, no semantic labels), and complexity analysis are all provided.

Practical impact: feed-forward inference (~12s per shape vs. 7-15 min for lifting methods), demonstrated downstream applications (interior editing, amodal segmentation with HoloPart), and strong qualitative results on AI-generated meshes with absent connectivity.
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination is not explicitly addressed: PartObjaverse-Tiny is derived from Objaverse, and the training corpus (500k shapes) is also curated from Objaverse. There is no stated decontamination check (e.g., filtering test shapes or near-duplicates from training data), which is important given the large reported margins. Performance on 3DCoMPaT++ and real-world scans partially mitigates this concern, but the omission should be fixed.

Heavy dependence on PartField: both encoder branches are initialized from PartField weights, and the second-stage data pipeline uses PartField pseudo-labels. The dual-branch architecture and SAM-like two-way decoder are competent engineering but largely combinations of known components (PVCNN, triplanes, SAM decoder, zero-conv). Novelty is primarily at the system/data level rather than in architectural innovation.
The interactive segmentation comparison (Table 1) only covers Point-SAM; iSeg (Lang et al., 2024), another interactive 3D segmentation method, is cited but not compared with quantitatively.

The annotation quality filter is heuristic and validated only qualitatively (Figure 15); no quantitative estimate of pseudo-label precision is given, and the claim that imperfect cases are 'negligible' is not directly measured.

Reproducibility concerns: the project page link is empty in the manuscript, and no code/data release commitment is visible; given the resource cost (8x H20 GPUs, 250k iterations) and the multi-stage data pipeline, reproduction without released artifacts would be difficult.

Some claims are slightly overstated, e.g., 'emergent open-world capabilities' — the 'Segment Every Part' mode is a designed NMS-based pipeline rather than a purely emergent behavior, and single-prompt IoU@1 of 56-60 on open-world data still leaves substantial room for improvement.
